Battleship. Heavily armored, large-displacement warships designed for direct combat at sea, serving as the capital ships of naval fleets from the age of steam onward. They represent the peak of naval dominance in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, before aircraft fundamentally shifted naval warfare. The battleship embodies an entire era of naval strategy and international power projection.

Battleships evolved from wooden sailing ships to ironclad vessels during the American Civil War. The encounter between the USS Monitor and the CSS Virginia revolutionized naval combat by proving that armored steam-powered ships could destroy traditional wooden warships. The HMS Dreadnought, launched in nineteen six, was the first all-big-gun battleship with uniform main armament. It sparked a global naval arms race as every major power raced to build modern dreadnoughts.

These vessels were characterized by thick armor plating, powerful main gun batteries, and exceptional displacement. The Yamato and USS Iowa were among the largest warships ever built. They dominated naval strategy through the early twentieth century, but Pearl Harbor on December seventh, nineteen forty-one, demonstrated both the battleship's vulnerability to air attack and its continued strategic importance in naval operations.

The Battle of the Coral Sea in nineteen forty-two marked a crucial turning point. It was the first naval battle where opposing ships never came within sight of each other. Aircraft did all the fighting, signaling the end of the battleship era. Battleships remained in limited service through the Cold War, fulfilling bombardment and power projection roles, but submarines and aircraft carriers became the dominant warship types. The battleship's reign had ended.
